subject: Chemistry
title: Road Salt: Melting Ice with Chemistry
description: A short lesson to help you apply Road Salt: Melting Ice with Chemistry.

hook.text: Spreading salt on icy roads lowers the freezing point of water, turning ice back into liquid.

buildup.text: Pure water freezes at 0°C. Dissolve sodium chloride in it and the freezing point drops to about -21°C.

discovery.text: Salt ions disrupt the crystal structure of ice. Water molecules can't organize into a solid as easily.

twist.text: Below -21°C, salt stops working. That's why northern countries use calcium chloride, which works down to -32°C.

climax.text: Road salt corrodes cars and poisons waterways. It costs billions in environmental damage annually.

punchline.text: Salt disrupts ice crystals. Simple chemistry that saves—and damages—roads.

quiz.question: How does road salt melt ice?
options: It lowers water's freezing point by disrupting ice crystal formation
It generates heat that melts the ice
It absorbs moisture from the air to dissolve ice

details.summary: Road salt lowers the freezing point of water through freezing point depression, a colligative property. When sodium chloride dissolves on ice, it disrupts the crystal lattice and creates a brine solution that remains liquid at temperatures below zero degrees Celsius.
details.whyItMatters: Freezing point depression is a fundamental colligative property used in winter road safety, food science, and industrial processes. Road salt represents the largest single use of salt worldwide.
takeaways: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point by disrupting ice crystal formation
Road salt is effective down to about minus 9 degrees Celsius
Alternatives like calcium chloride work at even lower temperatures

faq.question: Why does salt become less effective at very low temperatures?
faq.answer: Sodium chloride can only depress the freezing point to about minus 21 degrees Celsius for a saturated solution. Below about minus 9 degrees Celsius, it works too slowly to be practical on roads..

faq.question: Does road salt damage the environment?
faq.answer: Yes. Runoff carries dissolved salt into rivers, lakes, and groundwater, raising chloride levels that harm freshwater organisms. Salt also damages roadside vegetation, corrodes vehicles and bridges, and can contaminate drinking water supplies..
